source.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Xiang-Chen Song; Aashiq Muhamed; Yu-Jian Zheng; Ling-Jing Kong; Zeyu Tang; Mona T. Diab; Virginia Smith; Kun Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures run-to-run consistency of SAE feature dictionaries using PW-MCC, a different measurement from the original toy-model superposition work. It tests the stability aspect of V5, but not whether SAE features are complete or canonical.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own SAE dictionary-consistency and feature-alignment results. No rows are included for cited findings from other work or for hyperparameter values used only to select configurations. The tested metrics establish dictionary similarity or explanation similarity, not feature completeness or canonical status.
record.test_reason: The study measures run-to-run stability of SAE dictionaries (PW-MCC) on synthetic data and on Pythia-160M and Gemma-2-2B activations. That bears directly on V5's 'stable' component, using a method unlike the original toy-model work. It does not test completeness or canonicity, and does not test the geometry or polysemanticity versions (V1–V4, V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue that run-to-run consistency should be a standard SAE evaluation axis, and that high consistency is achievable (about 0.80 PW-MCC for TopK on LLMs). This is offered against the view that SAE features are only a pragmatic, non-unique decomposition. They note that consistency does not guarantee faithfulness or completeness, and that rare features remain less consistent.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures SAE dictionary alignment across independent training runs using assignment-based PW-MCC; it does not reproduce the original Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Consistency varies with SAE architecture, training progress, dictionary capacity relative to ground-truth feature count, activation frequency, and (in the synthetic analysis) cluster structure. Gemma-2-2B JumpReLU consistency is higher than its Pythia-160M result.

fits_no_version.finding: In compressive synthetic SAEs, dictionary capacity goes to frequent feature clusters superlinearly (Di ∝ p^β, β ≈ 1.26–1.46), and rare clusters are under-recovered.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs allocate dictionary capacity superlinearly to frequent features, so rare features are learned less stably. This concerns SAE allocation, not the underlying model's own neurons, so it is not V2.

fits_no_version.finding: Dictionary-vector cosine similarity of matched pairs tracks LLM-rated explanation similarity, from 1.71 in the lowest bucket to 8.28 in the highest.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vector-level SAE consistency corresponds to consistency of the automated explanations.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 1: Long Papers)
record.problems: LLM PW-MCC results are based on only 3 seeds for Pythia-160M and 2 seeds for Gemma-2-2B. PW-MCC measures vector alignment rather than functional faithfulness or completeness. Generated explanation similarity is rated by an LLM and is described as a partial proxy. The paper reports some differing approximate Pythia-160M values between Appendix F.1.2 and F.2.
record.rows_left_out: The paper includes additional figure-only synthetic sweeps and per-cluster/Zipf analyses in Appendix D, training curves in Figure 6, and additional feature-frequency plots in Appendix F. These were not separately extracted because the retained rows capture the reported numeric consistency results and the figure-only panels do not provide additional independently stated numerical values in the text.

untested.parts: Completeness, atomicity and canonical status of SAE features. Stability across datasets, base models or domains: only the seed varies, per the Limitations section. Functional faithfulness of the features.
Not tested. The synthetic data is a planted sparse dictionary, not a study of how a toy network stores features; no geometry or phase transition is examined.
Not tested. Neuron polysemanticity is not measured.
Not tested. The study does not examine whether LLM features are spread across neurons or whether SAEs recover true features in LLMs.

missing.what: The two-phase Zipf model shows frequency-dependent inter-run similarity, and the trend strengthens with dictionary size (80 to 10,000). Figure-only, no numbers.
Misspecifying k relative to the true sparsity degrades recovery, more sharply when k is too small; over-large k raises selection ambiguity. GT-MCC is shown only in a figure.
The paper reports the matched-regime synthetic GT-MCC for TopK as 0.97 versus 0.63 for Standard, though Figure 2 says PW-MCC for TopK reaches 1.0. A researcher should note this small inconsistency.

record.verdict_notes: This is a position paper. The LLM results are best-of-sweep, selected on PW-MCC itself, with 3 seeds for Pythia and 2 for Gemma. It is not an original source for V5. The reader swapped Table 1 and Table 2 count columns in rows r9–r13. Rows r28–r32 validate the metric rather than measure stability, so they were unlinked from V5.

versions.untested_parts: The synthetic capacity experiments measure recovery and run-to-run dictionary consistency, but do not test the claimed overlapping, nearly orthogonal geometry, sparsity-dependent superposition transition, or regular geometric arrangements.
The study does not measure neuron polysemanticity or test whether features compete for dimensions in neurons.
The study does not test non-capacity causes of polysemantic neurons.

The LLM experiments assess agreement between SAE dictionaries trained on activations, not whether LLM features are spread across neurons or whether SAE features recover the model's underlying features.

The study measures run-to-run dictionary consistency and similarity of generated explanations. It does not establish feature completeness, functional faithfulness, or canonical status across architectures, datasets, or models.
The study compares individual dictionary vectors but does not test whether the underlying model features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

relation.reason: The study reports its own measurements of dictionary stability on synthetic data and fixed LLM activations.

tranche.reason: Assignment-based comparisons across independent SAE runs directly test V5's stability component using a different method from the original superposition experiments.

source_check.notes: LLM results are configurations selected for highest final PW-MCC, with three Pythia seeds and two Gemma seeds; BatchTopK had not saturated. Explanation-similarity measurements provide a semantic proxy, but dictionary-wide functional or causal equivalence, completeness, and canonicity remain unestablished.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: TopK SAE dictionaries in the reported synthetic matched-capacity setting and on Pythia-160M and Gemma-2-2B activations
reader_labels.reason: TopK dictionaries show high run-to-run alignment, including PW-MCC of 0.8181 on Pythia-160M, 0.7898 on Gemma-2-2B, and convergence to 1.0 in the matched synthetic setting (r1, r14, r21). This supports stability in these tested settings, not feature completeness or canonical status.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Across SAE architectures, capacity regimes, and feature-frequency bins tested
reader_labels.reason: Consistency varies substantially by architecture and capacity; rare-feature similarity is lower than frequent-feature similarity, and the authors explicitly caution that high consistency does not guarantee completeness or faithfulness (r2-r4, r9-r20, r22-r27).
